segments.text: Good morning. Today we're going to look at forensic linguistics.
So first of all, what is forensic linguistics?
The Oxford English Dictionary defines forensic as pertaining to,
concerned with, or used in courts of law.
forensic linguistics then is the application of linguistic methods to
these areas. The study of forensic linguistics can be divided into two main
areas. Firstly, the language of the law and judicial processes, for example
questioning in the courtroom and the language in documents which set out the
law, and secondly, the language of evidence. For example, ransom notes and
spoken texts. To give you an idea of how forensic linguistics has been used, we're
going to look at four legal cases. Firstly, there is the case of a doctor
named Harold Shipman, who was convicted in January 2000 of the murder of 15 of
his patients. Shipman forged the last will and testament of one of his
patients, Mrs Kathleen Grundy, and this led to his arrest. Mrs Grundy's daughter,
Mrs Angela Woodruff, was a lawyer and had drawn up her mother's original will. When
a new will was discovered, she became suspicious. The choice of individual
words and the signature were different from her mother's usual style and the
document contained some uncharacteristic errors. As a consequence of her
suspicions, a forensic document examiner was employed to compare the alleged
signature on the will with her driving license which contained her authentic
signature. Significant differences were found. For example, the letter D in
Grundy was written with an open loop and was taller than in the authentic
signature. The evidence from the handwriting analysis helped convict
Shipman. The second case we will discuss concerns Dan Brown, the author of a book
called The Davinci Code. The Davinci Code is a best-selling book with over 4.5
million copies sold up to the 11th of December 2010. Brown was alleged to have
copied the central theme for the Da Vinci Code from an earlier non-fictional
book called The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail. In 2006 the judge ruled that
there had been no copying of text or the central themes.
Copyright infringement and plagiarism are areas where forensic linguistics can help solve
legal cases.
The third case concerns the protection of trademarks, and in particular protection for
the Google name.
This asks the question, how far can companies claim to own a word or a series of words?
And do these companies have the right to say who can and who cannot use these words?
Google fear that there is a risk that the word Google could become so commonly used that
it would become synonymous with the word search.
this happens they will not be able to protect their trademark. This in turn
could then lead to other people using the word Google to refer to their own
products. Their brand has a significant financial value and this would decrease
as a result. The last case we will look at is about how voices are unique. In
In this case, a recording made 25 years earlier was compared with a recently arrested suspect's voice to see if the suspect made the original recording.
The case uses forensic phonetics or voice analysis in order to identify the speaker.
The Yorkshire Ripper case concerned a serial killer who murdered 10 women between 1975 and 1979.
In 1979, the police received a tape recording, supposedly from the Yorkshire Ripper.
The police asked a Phonistician from Leeds University, Stanley Ellis,
to identify exactly where the speaker came from geographically. Ellis said that
the speaker came from Sunderland in the north-east of England originally, but
could not be sure that he still lived there. As a result, the police only
considered suspects with north-eastern accents. In 1981 Peter Sutcliffe, a lorry driver from
Bradford, was arrested and confessed to the murders. He was convicted shortly afterwards.
He did not have a north-eastern accent. In 2005, 26 years after the tapes had been sent,
a man from Sunderland, John Humble, was arrested and charged with sending the tapes to the police.
DNA from the envelope received by the police in 1979 was matched to a sample from John Humble.
Humble was also asked to read out a tape script of the original recordings and a comparison was
made by voice analysts. Humble was convicted of sending the false information
claiming to be the Yorkshire Ripper to the police.
